proposed_edges.relationship: Critiques address both Wolfe's model and its subsequent uses: Macoun and Strakosch question structural inevitability; Rowse questions a teleology of elimination; Englert directly challenges elimination as the defining logic. Kauanui defends Wolfe against formulaic citation while rejecting the replacement of Indigenous Studies (2013–20)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Macoun and Strakosch 2013 (author version, read): "SCT can depict colonization as structurally inevitable"; "Foundational scholar Patrick Wolfe has been labelled 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world'"; "a kind of colonial fatalism"; "it does not account for Indigenous lives". Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014 (read): "treating settler colonialism as a meta-structure, thus erasing both its contingency and the dynamics that co-constitute" it. Rowse 2014 (abstract, existing): a "teleology of elimination". Kauanui 2016 (read in full): a criticism of Wolfe's reception rather than of Wolfe, defending the theory against the phrase that 'often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement' with it, and asking that "Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies". 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' is the citation graph's category for a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position (Sol review 1.156, finding 3). Englert 2020 (read in full): "a critique of the Wolfe-an model"; elimination "does not accurately define the overall logic of settler colonialism, as claimed by Wolfe". Fairness: Kauanui and Goeman record his disclaimers and his engagement with NAIS; Macoun and Strakosch call his contribution "vital". (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Settler colonialism against underdevelopment: the 1970s–80s 'settler/dominion capitalism' literature made the settler colony 'the opposite of colonialism and associated underdevelopment' (Veracini 2013 on Denoon 1983); Englert returns the question through Harvey's accumulation by dispossession (2020)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Veracini 2013 (abstract, existing record; author manuscript read): in the third phase "settler colonialism is understood as the opposite of colonialism and associated underdevelopment and political fragmentation", and the settler-capitalism approach wrote "indigenous people and indigenous history off the conceptual map". Denoon 1983 at title level (existing). Englert 2020 (read in full): accumulation by dispossession "as developed by David Harvey (2003)" proposed as the alternative to the elimination model, with Emmanuel's 1972 NLR essay on white-settler colonialism in his bibliography. A comparison of frames; no descent asserted. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: The settler order as a frame for Canadian working-class history (Burrill 2019); settler workers as participants in 'accumulation by dispossession' who 'fight simultaneously over the distribution of wealth generated through their labour and the distribution of the colonial loot' (Englert 2020)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Burrill 2019 (abstract, existing record screq_burrill_2019; the strand cdn_working_class/indigenous_labour_settler_order carries him). Englert 2020 (read in full), conclusion: settler labour movements "fight simultaneously over the distribution of wealth generated through their labour and the distribution of the colonial loot accumulated through the dispossession of the indigenous population"; his cases are Palestine and South Africa, so the Canadian application is Burrill's. Re-proposes row 7 of the 2026-10-12 request, which is not on disk. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Land as 'settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element': agriculture 'is inherently sedentary and, therefore, permanent' and 'progressively eats into Indigenous territory, a primitive accumulation that turns native flora and fauna into a dwindling resource' (Wolfe 2006); 'land is the irreducible element of settler colonialism' (Snelgrove et al. 2014)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), fourth section: "Of itself, however, modernity cannot explain the insatiable dynamic whereby settler colonialism always needs more land. The answer that springs most readily to mind is agriculture"; "Agriculture not only supports the other sectors. It is inherently sedentary and, therefore, permanent"; "The reproach of nomadism renders the native removable." Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014, p. 30 (read): "land is the irreducible element of settler colonialism, and … environmental degradation has often proceeded through and in support of settler colonialism". Tuck and Yang 2012, p. 5 (read): "Within settler colonialism, the most important concern is land/water/air/subterranean earth". The dissertation evidence for the pairing is in the entry's scope_note, not here. Drawn by Agent B by the coordinator's decision; Agent C does not duplicate it. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

verification.note: Read in full on 2026-10-23 (the journal's own 2011 PDF, "© settler colonial studies 1 (2011), ISSN 1838-0743", deposited by the author under CC BY-NC-ND 3.0; handle 1959.3/156165). Passages: "you, work for me" against "you, go away" (p. 1); "settler colonialism, by contrast, extinguishes itself" and "the structure persistently pursues a specific end point" (p. 3, note 11 citing Wolfe 1999, p. 163); postcolonial studies "failed to detect the settler colonial 'situation' in its specific operation" (p. 5); "Decolonisation is not settler decolonisation" (p. 5); "impervious to regime change" quoted from Wolfe (p. 5); "settler colonialism ends with an indigenous ultimate permanence" (p. 7); the politics of recognition "cannot be considered a genuinely decolonising move" (p. 8); "Reconciliation should be a practice and not a process" (p. 9); ARC grant DP0986984 (acknowledgements).
